text:
this was a good question

re: "the market is always right" in #8

"I hate that comment, 'the market is wrong here.' The market is never wrong. When you own a stock that you think is worth X and is trading half of X, you're wrong. Something is missing. You find out later what it was. The market is always right and it tells you it is right." 

the full quote is below, manager named effron

so, this is clearly nuanced and there's no right answer, just schools of thought

boils down to: do u see red as risk, or red as opportunity...is down 20% "drawdown" or "back the truck up."

there are brilliant investors on both sides

the quote to me, I view as a default position/way of operating

and to me, this pairs with Buffett's 20 hole punchcard

you are not as smart as you think, you don't have as many good ideas as you think, overconfidence bias

everything re: efficiency is correct, but its the frequency of finding "opportunities" that is debated

most people don't do enough work to understand the market-implied/consensus view

they just see a stock that seems cheap

lot of times, stocks have taken a rocky road...there's damage to mgmt credibility, questionable margin flow-thru, no fcf, stocks have narratives and overhangs which affect why they are where they are.

if you are a sharp analyst who does real work, a lot of the time your correct conclusion after months of research should be, "its fairly priced"

not "I need ideas, and I just spent months on this, so its a long or a short"...which is what ends up happening.

biases/errors at work, now u have $ in a coin-flip bet, fairly valued stock, bc u couldnt just say the market had it right.

so as a default way of operating -- "mkt is right" as null hypothesis -- generating a new idea requires real effort, u have a lot to disprove for it to be a long or short

ur not just wandering into shit

and then the quote "if you say its worth X and its trading half X, you're wrong" -- out of 100 times, probably 90-95 of those, the quote is gonna be spot on

its not either/or (is the mkt efficient or inefficient) -- its understanding how rare a truly mispriced bet is, then sizing it, and then I think druck has a quote (along the lines of "invest first, investigate later") to the extent of.... shit only stays mispriced for 2-3 months. you have to move fast and with incomplete information.

as a rule of thumb, I think "actionable ideas generated" runs inverse with experience... a new trader has 500 ideas a day, a guy with 30 years experience sits on his hands all day, doing nothing, waiting for the perfect setup.

same principle

full quote/tweet below...I agree with everything written, and every great risk manager I've seen, they all operate this way

https://t.co/60mnaeVujI

quotedTweet.text: @gregoryblotnick I like most of these, but I don't get number 8. Isn't the entire job knowing something that the market doesn't (market inefficiency) with the understanding that the market may disprove or eventually reflect your opinion (market efficiency)?
